title: Making EU Trade Agreements Work: The Role of Rules of Origin
journal: World Scientific Studies in International Economics
abstract: A key element of the EU's free trade and preferential trade agreements is the extent to which they deliver improved market access and so contribute to the EU's foreign policy objectives towards developing countries and neighbouring countries in Europe, including the countries of the Balkans. Previous preferential trade schemes have been ineffective in delivering improved access to the EU market since only a small proportion of the available preferences have actually been utilised. The main reason for this is probably the very restrictive rules of origin that the EU imposes, coupled with the costs of proving consistency with these rules. If the EU wants the 'Everything but Arms' agreement and free trade agreements with countries in the Balkans to generate substantial improvements in access to the EU market for products from these countries then it will have to reconsider the current rules of origin and implement less restrictive rules backed up by a careful safeguards policy.
summary_en: EU free-trade and preferential agreements with developing and neighbouring countries (Balkans, ACP states, 'Everything but Arms') often deliver less market access than promised. Brenton and Manchin show why: highly restrictive EU rules of origin, plus the cost of proving compliance, render most preference margins effectively unusable. Only a small share of available preferences are claimed in practice. The paper recommends substantial liberalisation of rules of origin combined with careful safeguards to make EU preferential agreements actually deliver on their stated objectives.
data_used: EU preference utilisation data from Eurostat, covering bilateral preference-eligible trade flows under 'Everything but Arms' and other EU preferential agreements; product-level analysis of rules-of-origin restrictiveness.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian KKM and EU DG-TRADE when negotiating or revising EU preferential agreements. Also relevant for HIPA in advising Hungarian exporters about realistic market access under EU preferences for developing-country partners.
